explanations.explanation: David leans in and says, "…for I am poor and needy." No résumé, no list of favors, just "I need help." I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so I know how honest that feels. I think it's a mighty fine way to knock on God's door.
Not a chance, baker. David doesn't flex one muscle in this prayer. The reason he gives is that he is poor and needy (Psalm 86:1). The strong-and-brave speech never makes it into the psalm.

explanations.answer: He has served God for years
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like a reasonable thing to say, but David doesn't say it here. The reason in verse 1 is simple: "…for I am poor and needy." He doesn't hand God a service record or ask for a gold star. He just says what he needs.
Once in a while? Oh no, friend. David says, "…for I call to You all day long." That's all day, not a quick check-in. The man has the Lord on speed dial and he's wearing out the button.
Right, it's false. David says, "…for I call to You all day long." That's the opposite of once in a while. All day means all day, and I love it.

David says, "For You, O Lord, are kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You." Kind and forgiving, that's the word he picks. Look at that last part: the loving devotion is for all who call on Him. I'd keep calling too.

Proud and distant isn't what David says. He says the Lord is "…kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You." Those are his words for the Lord, and they're a long way from proud.
David says the opposite, baker. In verse 15 he calls the Lord "…slow to anger…" And here in verse 5 he says the Lord is "…kind and forgiving…"

David says, "In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me." That's his reason. He calls because he knows Someone picks up. Plenty of people call a customer service line with no idea if anyone ever will.
Owes would make it a bill, and David isn't sending God an invoice. He asks for mercy and says he calls because the Lord answers him (Psalm 86:7). A gift and a debt are two very different things.
David doesn't say that. His reason is simple: "…because You answer me." He calls in his day of distress, and he says the Lord answers. That's the whole line.

David says, "All the nations You have made will come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name." Think about that. One man in one prayer, and he's looking at every nation. He starts small and ends up looking at the whole planet.
A temple is a big idea, but David doesn't say it here. He says the nations "…will come and bow before You, O Lord…" The psalm talks about bowing, not building.

Gold would look nice, but it's not in the verse. David says the nations will "…come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name." What he describes is bowing and glorifying, with no gift table in sight.
David says, "For You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God." He doesn't say God is one of a few. He doesn't say God is the best of the bunch. He says God alone is God.
It's the other way around, friend. David says, "You alone are God." Right before that he says God is great and performs wonders. This psalm isn't taking a vote.

David prays, "Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth." He wants to be taught and then to walk in it. Learning without walking is like reading the recipe and never turning on the oven. David wants both.

Secrets sound exciting, but that's not the word. David says, "Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth." The word he uses is way. He asks to be taught it so that he may walk in God's truth.

David has enemies in this psalm, so I see why battles came to mind. But he prays, "Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth." The word he uses is way, not battles. He asks to be taught it so that he may walk in God's truth.

explanations.answer: So that he may fear God's name
explanations.explanation: David prays, "Give me an undivided heart, that I may fear Your name." That's what he wants it for. He asks for an undivided heart, and fearing God's name is the reason he gives.

explanations.answer: So that he may rule with wisdom
explanations.explanation: It's an easy guess, but the verse doesn't say it. David asks for an undivided heart "…that I may fear Your name." Ruling with wisdom isn't the reason he gives.

explanations.answer: So that he may forget his troubles
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask to forget a thing. He doesn't hide from his troubles, either. He talks about them in this very psalm. What he asks for is an undivided heart "…that I may fear Your name."

explanations.answer: Delivered him from the depths of Sheol
explanations.explanation: David says, "You have delivered me from the depths of Sheol." That's a heavy line. And he says it right after calling God's loving devotion to him great. I think David isn't saying it lightly.

explanations.answer: Set him high upon a rock
explanations.explanation: That's a nice picture, but it's not in this psalm. David says God "…delivered me from the depths of Sheol." He's talking about being brought up from deep down.

explanations.answer: Given him rest from all his foes
explanations.explanation: David still has foes in this psalm. In the very next verse, arrogant men rise against him (Psalm 86:14). What he says here is that God has "…delivered me from the depths of Sheol."

Yes, and look where he says it. Right after ruthless men come after him, David says, "But You, O Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness." He looks at the trouble and then at God. I want that kind of focus.
It's true, baker. Right after the ruthless men show up, David says "But You, O Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger…" He doesn't let the trouble change who he says God is.

David asks, "Show me a sign of Your goodness, that my enemies may see and be ashamed…" He wants the very people against him to see it. And he says the Lord has helped him and comforted him (Psalm 86:17). He's asking from experience.
David does call himself God's servant in this psalm, so that word is in the neighborhood. But the sign is for his enemies. He says, "…that my enemies may see and be ashamed…"
No brothers in this psalm, friend. David asks for a sign of God's goodness "…that my enemies may see and be ashamed…" Enemies are the ones he names there.
David ends the other way. His last words say, "for You, O LORD, have helped me and comforted me." Helped and comforted. The psalm ends on that note, and it makes my mustache curl.

That's right, it's false. David ends with, "for You, O LORD, have helped me and comforted me." He started this prayer poor and needy, and he finishes by saying God helped. I'd close a prayer like that every time.
